passages.t: A search for a new queen
passages.happening:
‘Some time later, when the anger of King Xerxes had subsided, he remembered Vashti and what she had done, and what had been decreed against her’ (verse 1).

His attendants make a proposal: “Let a search be made for beautiful young virgins for the king” (verse 2). Commissioners in every province are to gather them into the harem at Susa, under the care of Hegai, the king's eunuch in charge of the women. ‘Then let the young woman who pleases the king become queen in place of Vashti’ (verse 4). The king likes the idea, and he acts on it.
passages.hearers:
Four years pass between the feast of chapter 1 and Esther's night with the king. In between, Greek sources tell of Xerxes' invasion of Greece and his defeats at Salamis in 480 BC and Plataea in 479 BC. The book says nothing of them. It says only, some time later.

Notice what the king remembers: Vashti, what she had done, and the decree he cannot take back. The search for a new queen is the attendants' answer to a king who may regret his own law.

Persian kings kept large harems. The young women gathered from the provinces were not asked. They were taken.
passages.later: Daniel and his friends were also taken young into a foreign king's palace and given Babylonian names: ‘The chief official gave them new names’ (Daniel 1:7).
passages.asks: The plan was made by powerful men for a powerful man, and young women paid the cost. Ask whose costs are hidden in the comforts of the powerful in your own world. And ask what it would take to notice them.

passages.t: An orphan taken into the palace and made queen
passages.happening:
‘Now there was at the citadel of Susa a Jewish man from the tribe of Benjamin named Mordecai son of Jair, the son of Shimei, the son of Kish’ (verse 5). His family had been carried into exile from Jerusalem with Jeconiah king of Judah (verse 6). ‘And Mordecai had brought up Hadassah (that is, Esther), the daughter of his uncle, because she did not have a father or mother’ (verse 7). When her parents died, he took her in as his own daughter.

When the king's order is proclaimed and many young women are gathered, ‘Esther was also taken to the palace and placed under the care of Hegai, the custodian of the women’ (verse 8). She wins Hegai's favor, and he gives her the best place in the harem. ‘Esther did not reveal her people or her lineage, because Mordecai had instructed her not to do so’ (verse 10). Every day Mordecai walks in front of the harem court to learn how she is.

Each young woman spends twelve months in beauty treatments before her turn to go to the king. She goes in the evening, and in the morning she goes to a second harem, the house of the concubines, and she does not go to the king again unless he delights in her and calls her by name (verses 12-14).

Esther is taken to the king in the tenth month of his seventh year (verse 16). ‘And the king loved Esther more than all the other women’ (verse 17), and he sets the royal crown on her head and makes her queen in place of Vashti. He gives a great banquet, Esther's banquet (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
The tenth month of Xerxes' seventh year is about 479 or 478 BC.

Mordecai's family line ties him to the tribe of Benjamin and to an ancestor named Kish, the name of King Saul's father. That will matter when his enemy is named an Agagite in chapter 3. His family was carried away with Jeconiah, also called Jehoiachin, in 597 BC. Since that was more than a century before, most readers take verse 6 to mean that his great-grandfather Kish was exiled, and the Hebrew allows it.

His name is related to Marduk, the chief god of Babylon, and Esther's Persian name may be related to a word for star or to the goddess Ishtar. Many Jews in the east bore local names alongside Hebrew ones, as Daniel and his friends did. Her Hebrew name, Hadassah, means myrtle.

The book describes the harem plainly and without romance. A young woman taken into it did not choose to go and could not choose to leave. Her year of treatments was part of a system run by eunuchs, and after one night with the king she might spend the rest of her life in the house of the concubines without seeing him again. Esther was one of many young women whose lives were shaped this way, an orphan from a scattered and powerless people.

The book's rescue begins with an act of care. Mordecai took in his orphaned cousin as his own daughter, and he walked past the harem every day to ask after her. And twice the book says that Esther kept her people hidden on his instruction (verses 10 and 20). The reader knows what no one in the palace knows.
passages.later: Mordecai's family went into exile in the deportation that Second Kings records: ‘Jehoiachin king of Judah, his mother, his servants, his commanders, and his officials all surrendered to the king of Babylon’ (2 Kings 24:12). And Kish was the name of Saul's father, a Benjamite ‘whose name was Kish son of Abiel’ (1 Samuel 9:1).
passages.hard:
What should a reader make of young women taken into the king's harem, and of Esther among them?

The coercion is real, and the book does not hide it. Esther ‘was also taken’ (verse 8). She was almost certainly given no choice in being brought to the palace, and refusing the king would have been fatal. Readers have long been troubled by her situation. Unlike Daniel, who would not eat the king's food, Esther enters the harem, spends a night with a pagan king, and marries him, all while hiding that she is a Jew.

Some interpreters criticize Esther and Mordecai for compromise. They see ambition in Mordecai and blending in on Esther's part, and they note that the book never praises their choices in this chapter. Others point out how little choice Esther had, and that hiding who she was may have been a sensible protection in a dangerous court.

The text itself is restrained and does not moralize. It shows people living as a vulnerable minority under a foreign empire, making choices under pressure. It does not call what was done to these young women right, and these notes do not either. Readers need not approve every step to see God's hand in the whole story.

A word for anyone who has been sold, traded, or forced to work or to do sexual acts by someone who controls them, or who is in that place now. It is not your fault. You are not the property of the people who hold you. If you can, please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Mordecai took in a child who had no one, and kept asking after her when she was out of reach. Ask who in your life has no father or mother to watch over them. And ask what it would mean to keep asking after someone you can no longer protect.

passages.happening:
‘In those days, while Mordecai was sitting at the king’s gate, Bigthan and Teresh, two of the king’s eunuchs who guarded the entrance, grew angry and conspired to assassinate King Xerxes’ (verse 21).

Mordecai learns of it and tells Queen Esther, and she tells the king in Mordecai's name (verse 22). ‘After the report had been investigated and verified, both officials were hanged on the gallows. And all this was recorded in the Book of the Chronicles in the presence of the king’ (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
Sitting at the king's gate probably means that Mordecai held an official post. In the ancient Near East the gate of a city or palace was where officials did business and justice was given. That would explain how he heard of the plot.

The danger was real. Xerxes himself was later killed in a plot by his own court officials in 465 BC.

Mordecai saves the king's life and receives no reward. But the deed is written down. Herodotus describes the Persian custom of recording the names of those who served the king well as royal benefactors. A reader who knows the rest of the story knows that this record will be read on exactly the right night, in chapter 6.
passages.later: In Acts, a young man learns of a plot to kill Paul and reports it, and the plot fails: ‘But when the son of Paul’s sister heard about the plot, he went into the barracks and told Paul’ (Acts 23:16).
passages.asks: Mordecai did the right thing and was forgotten. Ask whether you can do good when no one notices or thanks you. And ask what record God keeps that you cannot see.
